Issued at 1240 PM CDT Sun Sep 13 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: Another cool, but pleasant early Fall day in 
the region as continued mid-lvl clouds cross the CWA. With a 
light east southeast wind, we'll continue to see temperatures 
rise towards the upper 60s. 

TONIGHT: Two thirds of the overnight hours are expected to remain 
quiet.  However as we move past midnight, a steady increase in a 
broad LLJ through the Plains, along with the approach of mid-lvl 
vorticity will begin to develop showers and thunderstorms. Two 
areas of focus for convection will develop through the morning. 
One area will be across central and north central South Dakota, 
with a second band of elevated convection forming from south 
central South Dakota into eastern Nebraska where strong theta-e 
advection begins to move northeast. While widespread severe 
weather isn't anticipated, soundings show elevated CAPE around 
1500 J/KG through the CWA. Mid- lvl lapse rates are marginal, 
but shear could be strong enough for a few storms briefly 
capable of quarter size hail. 

MONDAY: Ongoing convection at daybreak Monday will continue to 
move northeast during the morning hours. HREF/NBM mean QPF 
suggests fairly widespread 0.25-0.50" totals by mid-day, but the
ceiling is also quite high with outside potential for an inch 
of rain in very isolated locations. While the initial band of 
moderate rain will move away from the CWA by early afternoon, 
model consensus keeps the orientation of the LLJ favorable to 
allow persistent showers or even isolated thunderstorms well 
into the afternoon. Depending on cloud cover, a very narrow 
window for surface based convection will still be possible by 
mid/late afternoon as a surface warm front attempts to lift 
northward. While most guidance has backed off on the northward 
extent of destabilization and kept this south of Highway 20, a 
few models remain steadfast that upwards of 2000+ J/KG MLCAPE 
could develop from Sioux City to Storm Lake by 23Z. A quick 
upscale growth situation would then develop as lift is maximized
with an approaching mid-lvl vort. IF storms could develop, all 
hazards would be possible initially, with activity rapidly 
shifting SE early in the evening. 

The persistent cloud cover and development of widespread low stratus 
will leave cooler temperatures over the CWA. I have again attempted 
to lower highs towards the cooler side of NBM guidance. Barring a 
late afternoon jump if clouds scatter, most locations especially 
east of I-29 may struggle to reach 70 degrees and those in Southwest 
Minnesota could still be too warm with their forecast highs. 

One final item of note for Monday will be winds.  A sharpening of 
the SPG through the morning will promote sustained winds as high as 
20 mph at times.  Gusts, especially behind departing rain, may rise 
into the 30 to 40 mph range into early afternoon. 

TUESDAY-WEDNESDAY:  High pressure arrives for Tuesday, signaling dry 
conditions in most locations with continued slightly cooler than 
normal high temperatures.  A slight shift of mid-lvl flow back to 
the southwest by Wednesday could bring enough moisture return for 
scattered showers in most areas during the day Wednesday. The focus 
of the strongest moisture return, and resultant risk for heavier 
precipitation continue to stay focused south of Highway 20. 

THURSDAY-SUNDAY: Shortwave ridging moves back through the Plains for 
Thursday and early Friday, spelling a return of dry conditions and 
some potential for temperatures to return to normal levels to 
finish the week. As alluded to in yesterday's discussion, 
signals remain favorable for rain by Friday as a stronger wave 
ejects out of the Southern Rockies and into the Plains. Still 
lots of details to work out with this system, but as expected, 
the 24 hr probabilities for >0.25" ending Saturday morning have 
jumped over 50% in all three major ensembles. Quite a bit of 
uncertainty for next weekend in regards to the eventual shift 
of mid-lvl flow. Ensembles showing low percentage PoPs over a 
large area suggesting a significant spread in guidance. While 
severe weather risks are expected to remain low, temperatures 
stay near seasonal normals with an 8 degree spread in the 
25/75th percentile data split either side of normal.
